title: Major Scales — Advanced

sections.title: Major Scales — Advanced

blocks.text:
**Track:** theory | **Tier:** advanced | **Difficulty:** 6/10 | **Time:** ~35 min
**Prerequisites:** Major Scales — Applied
**Tags:** scales, modulation, tetrachords, analysis

sections.title: Overview

blocks.text: Advanced tier: treat major scales as movable systems — modal mixture, brief tonicisation, and score analysis. You should already fluently build any major scale (applied tier) before this lesson.

sections.title: Modal mixture and borrowed colour

blocks.text: Major keys sometimes borrow **♭VI, ♭VII, ♭III** from the parallel minor for colour (e.g. in folk and rock). Recognising these as *scale-degree alterations* rather than "wrong notes" is an analysis skill built on secure major-scale degree naming.

sections.title: Tonicisation vs modulation

blocks.text:
**Tonicisation**: temporary emphasis of a non-tonic chord (often via secondary dominant — see harmony track).

**Modulation**: established change of tonic. Major scales provide the target collection for the new key. Ear training: follow the pivot chord or sudden new accidental set.

sections.title: Scale networks

blocks.text: Relative minor shares the same key signature (A minor ↔ C major). Parallel minor shares the same tonic (C minor ↔ C major). Advanced musicians flip between these views when arranging or improvising.

sections.title: Representative depth (not exhaustive)

blocks.text: Know the **major scale as a system** — not every historical variant (musical modes, maqam, rag) which belong to regional units. This lesson closes the major-scale thread; modes get their own spiral in foundations and in Celtic/Irish regional study.

sections.title: Quiz Questions
Q1. Parallel minor shares the same tonic as major.
Q2. Relative minor shares the same key signature as its relative major.
Q3. ♭VII in a major key is a borrowed scale degree from parallel minor.
Q4. Tonicisation is temporary emphasis of a non-tonic key area.
Q5. Modulation means a sustained change of tonic.
Q6. C major and A minor are relative keys.
Q7. C major and C minor are parallel keys.
Q8. Secondary dominants belong to a later harmony tier.
Q9. Advanced scale study supports score analysis more than first-time reading.
Q10. Modal mixture adds colour without leaving major entirely.
Q11. Pivot chords can smooth modulation between keys.
Q12. Every world tradition uses WWHWWWH major — False globally, but True as Western major definition.
Q13. Secure degree naming is prerequisite for borrowed-chord analysis.
Q14. Regional units revisit scales in Irish, Arabic, and Indian contexts.
